why: The Plain English Translation follows NA28, whose text in the Catholic Letters is the Editio Critica Maior's; the word list shows that it is the only place in 3 John where NA28 and the SBL text differ. Without the article the line matches 1:3 ("you do walk in truth") and 2 John 1:4 ("walking in truth").
b: With the article, "the truth" is the faith itself, the road the children walk on; without it, "truth" describes how they walk. The difference is slight.

t: "I wrote something," "I would have written," or "I wrote"?
p: Copyists were uneasy that a letter of the Elder had been lost or refused, and changed the words.

readings.w: NA28, SBL, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort; Sinaiticus (first hand), Alexandrinus, 048, 1739, 2298; some Coptic copies, the Armenian; Jerome
Vaticanus (03); some Coptic copies
Sinaiticus as corrected, 33, 81, 614, 1505 and others; the Latin; Hilary
Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV "I wrote unto the church"); Ephraemi, K, L, P, Ψ, most later manuscripts

why: "I wrote something" has early support and explains the others. Plummer thought "I would have written" was a change made to avoid admitting that a letter from the apostle had been lost; dropping "something" makes the letter sound weightier. Vaticanus' "you wrote" is probably a slip of one letter.
b: Which letter is meant is debated. Most scholars, C. H. Dodd among them, think of a lost letter of recommendation, since 3 John says nothing of the dispute over teaching in 2 John; Plummer also ruled out 1 and 2 John. John Painter argues that it was 2 John.

t: "Those who want to" or "those who welcome them"?
